concepts.label: Apomorphine, a dopamine agonist given by subcutaneous injection, is used as rescue therapy for sudden "off" akinesia episodes in Parkinson disease
concepts.article_title: Apomorphine for off-akinesia rescue in Parkinson disease
concepts.definition: Apomorphine is a potent, non-selective dopamine (D1/D2) receptor agonist. Because oral levodopa's effect can wear off unpredictably in advanced Parkinson disease, producing sudden "off" periods of akinesia (inability to move), apomorphine is given by subcutaneous injection (or pump infusion) as rescue therapy: its rapid onset (minutes) restores mobility quickly until the next dose of oral medication takes effect. It is not used as first-line or maintenance therapy because of its short duration of action, need for parenteral administration, and prominent nausea (routinely co-prescribed with an antiemetic such as domperidone).
concepts.explicit_objective: State that apomorphine, a subcutaneously injected dopamine agonist, is used as rescue therapy for sudden off-akinesia episodes in Parkinson disease.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing apomorphine (a rapid-onset injectable rescue agent for acute off-episodes) with oral dopamine agonists such as pramipexole/ropinirole, which are used for maintenance therapy, not acute rescue.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 1 ("apomorphine / Rescue medication in Off Akinesia"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 1 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf (src_00b7644763f78f604253), p1.

concepts.label: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu-opioid receptor
concepts.article_title: Buprenorphine as a partial mu-opioid agonist
concepts.definition: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu-opioid receptor (and a kappa-receptor antagonist), unlike full agonists such as morphine or methadone. Because it only partially activates the mu receptor, it produces a "ceiling effect" on analgesia and respiratory depression, giving it a wider safety margin in overdose, and its high receptor affinity lets it displace full agonists, which can precipitate withdrawal if given too soon after another opioid. These properties make it useful both as an analgesic and, like methadone, as opioid substitution therapy for opioid use disorder.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu-opioid receptor, distinguishing it from full mu-agonists such as morphine and methadone.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing buprenorphine's partial agonism (ceiling effect, safer in overdose, can precipitate withdrawal if given too soon after a full agonist) with methadone's full agonism (no ceiling effect, used for maintenance without the precipitated-withdrawal risk).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 2 ("buprenorphine / Partial Mu Agonist"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, p1; the identical fact also appears as CNS Assessment 1's Pharmacology item 1 ("Bubrenurphine ----> partial mu agonist ?"), authored once here.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 2 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf (src_00b7644763f78f604253), p1, and again as CNS Assessment 1's Pharmacology item 1 (src_f59e62e45a06eee80102).

concepts.label: Amantadine, used to treat Parkinson disease, causes livedo reticularis as a characteristic adverse effect
concepts.definition: Amantadine, originally an antiviral, has antiparkinsonian activity (increasing dopamine release and blocking NMDA glutamate receptors) and is used both as monotherapy in early/mild Parkinson disease and as an add-on to reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesia. A characteristic, distinctive adverse effect is livedo reticularis: a mottled, lace-like, reddish-blue discoloration of the skin (usually the lower limbs), thought to relate to local catecholamine release affecting cutaneous blood vessels. It is generally reversible on stopping the drug.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that amantadine, used to treat Parkinson disease, causes livedo reticularis as a characteristic adverse effect.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing amantadine's livedo reticularis with benztropine's atropine-like anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision) — both are antiparkinsonian drugs but with distinct, drug-specific characteristic adverse effects.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 3 ("amantadine / Livido reticularis"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 3 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf (src_00b7644763f78f604253), p1.

concepts.label: Mossy fibres, the major cerebellar afferents, synapse on granule cell dendrites in the granular layer of the cerebellar cortex, not the molecular layer
concepts.article_title: Mossy fibre synapses in the cerebellar granular layer
concepts.definition: Mossy fibres are one of the two main classes of afferent input to the cerebellar cortex (the other being climbing fibres). They terminate in the innermost of the cerebellar cortex's three layers, the granular layer, where they synapse on the dendrites of granule cells to form characteristic glomeruli; granule cell axons then ascend to the molecular layer as parallel fibres, which synapse on Purkinje cell dendrites. Mossy fibres themselves are therefore not found in the molecular layer, and a mossy fibre's direct synaptic partner is the granule cell, not the Purkinje cell.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that mossy fibres synapse on granule cell dendrites in the granular layer of the cerebellar cortex, and are not found in the molecular layer.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing mossy fibres (terminate in the granular layer, synapse on granule cells) with climbing fibres (arise from the inferior olive, ascend through the granular layer to synapse directly on Purkinje cell dendrites in the molecular layer).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 6 ("mossy fibers / Not found in the molecular layer of the the cerebellum cortex"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, p1; complementary to CNS Assessment 1's Histology item 2 ("Dentreties of granule cell Synapse with mossy fibers"), merged into this one concept and authored once here.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 6 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf (src_00b7644763f78f604253), p1, and again (complementary phrasing) as CNS Assessment 1's Histology item 2 (src_f59e62e45a06eee80102).

concepts.label: The pterygomaxillary fissure is the opening through which the infratemporal fossa communicates with the pterygopalatine fossa
concepts.article_title: The pterygomaxillary fissure connecting infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae
concepts.definition: The pterygomaxillary fissure is a narrow vertical gap between the posterior surface of the maxilla and the pterygoid process of the sphenoid bone. It is the principal route by which the infratemporal fossa, laterally, communicates with the pterygopalatine fossa, medially, and transmits the terminal (third) part of the maxillary artery along with the maxillary nerve's branches as they pass into the pterygopalatine fossa. This makes it a key anatomical landmark linking the two fossae's neurovascular contents.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the pterygomaxillary fissure is the opening through which the infratemporal fossa communicates with the pterygopalatine fossa.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Trigeminal nerve and infratemporal region
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the pterygomaxillary fissure (infratemporal fossa to pterygopalatine fossa) with the lateral pterygoid plate (the medial bony boundary of the infratemporal fossa itself) — both are infratemporal-fossa landmarks but with different roles.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 31 ("ptrygemaxillary fissure (ass2) / bytfath infratemporal fossa 3ala al pterygopalatine fossa"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 31 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf (src_00b7644763f78f604253), p4, cross-referenced by the source to Assessment 2.

concepts.label: The buccal nerve is the only sensory branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve
concepts.article_title: The buccal nerve as the sole sensory branch of the mandibular nerve's anterior division
concepts.definition: The mandibular nerve (V3), the third division of the trigeminal nerve, divides into a small anterior division (mainly motor, supplying the muscles of mastication) and a larger posterior division (mainly sensory). The (long) buccal nerve is the single exception: it is the only sensory branch arising from the anterior division, supplying general sensation to the skin and mucous membrane of the cheek and the buccal gingiva of the lower molars — it carries no motor fibres and, despite its name, is unrelated to the facial nerve's motor buccal branches.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the buccal nerve is the only sensory branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Trigeminal nerve and infratemporal region
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the trigeminal (long) buccal nerve, a sensory branch of V3, with the facial nerve's buccal branches, which are motor branches supplying the buccinator and other muscles of facial expression.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 33 ("buccal nerve / The only sensory nerve from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 33 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf (src_00b7644763f78f604253), p4, cross-referenced by the source to Assessment 2.

concepts.label: Stimulation of the basal ganglia's indirect pathway disinhibits the subthalamic nucleus
concepts.article_title: Indirect pathway stimulation disinhibits the subthalamic nucleus
concepts.definition: The basal ganglia's indirect pathway runs from the striatum to the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe), which normally exerts tonic inhibitory (GABAergic) drive onto the subthalamic nucleus. When the indirect pathway is stimulated, striatal neurons inhibit the GPe; this inhibition of an inhibitory structure removes the GPe's restraint on the subthalamic nucleus, disinhibiting it, so subthalamic nucleus activity increases. The now more active subthalamic nucleus, in turn, excites the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi)/substantia nigra pars reticulata, increasing their inhibitory output to the thalamus and net-suppressing movement — the opposite overall effect to the direct pathway.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that stimulation of the basal ganglia's indirect pathway disinhibits the subthalamic nucleus by first inhibiting the external globus pallidus.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the indirect pathway's net effect (disinhibits the subthalamic nucleus, ultimately suppressing movement) with the direct pathway's net effect (inhibits the GPi/SNr directly, disinhibiting the thalamus and facilitating movement) — or with hemiballismus, which results from destructive subthalamic nucleus lesions rather than physiological indirect-pathway activation.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 48 ("disinhibtion of subthalamic nucleus / Result of stimulation of the indirect pathway in basal ganglia"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, p6.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 48 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf (src_00b7644763f78f604253), p6.

concepts.label: Thermal nociceptors are stimulated by skin temperatures above about 50 degC, and their brief stimulation by extreme cold can also evoke a paradoxical cold sensation
concepts.article_title: Thermal nociceptor thresholds and paradoxical cold sensation
concepts.definition: Thermal (heat) nociceptors are free nerve endings that begin firing only once skin temperature exceeds roughly 50 degC, the threshold at which tissue damage risk begins, distinguishing them from the separate warm and cold thermoreceptors that signal ordinary, non-painful temperature. A related phenomenon is paradoxical cold sensation: intense, rapid activation of cold-sensitive afferents (or, in some accounts, transient co-activation of cold-type fibres by extreme cold/heat) can be perceived as a brief, sharp "cold" sensation, an exception to the otherwise orderly heat-versus-cold coding of the thermal system.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that thermal nociceptors are stimulated by skin temperatures above about 50 degC.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing thermal nociceptors (fire only above ~50 degC, signal tissue-damaging heat) with ordinary warm thermoreceptors (signal a much lower, non-painful range of warming) — the two are distinct receptor populations with different thresholds and different perceptual qualities.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 49 ("thermal nociceptors / 7ad et3ras le daraget 7arara a3la men khamseen, stimulation to thermal noci receptors... Paradoxical cold sensation is rapid and transient"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, p6-7; the identical >50C fact also appears as CNS Assessment 1's Physiology item 5, authored once here.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 49 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf (src_00b7644763f78f604253), p6-7, and again as CNS Assessment 1's Physiology item 5 (src_f59e62e45a06eee80102).

concepts.label: Otitis media is a cause of extracranial headache
concepts.article_title: Otitis media as a cause of extracranial headache
concepts.definition: Extracranial headache is referred or locally generated pain arising from pain-sensitive structures outside the cranial cavity (scalp, sinuses, teeth, ears, cervical spine, temporomandibular joint, and so on), as opposed to intracranial causes (meningeal irritation, raised or lowered CSF pressure, vascular structures). Otitis media, inflammation/infection of the middle ear, is a classic example: the inflamed, pressurised middle ear generates pain that is perceived as headache, mediated by the sensory innervation of the ear (branches of the trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves) rather than by any intracranial mechanism.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that otitis media is a recognised cause of extracranial headache.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing otitis media (an extracranial cause of headache, from middle-ear inflammation) with intracranial causes such as meningeal irritation or a change in CSF pressure, which act through entirely different pain-sensitive structures inside the skull.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 52 ("otitis media / Is a cause of extracranial headache"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, p7.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 52 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf (src_00b7644763f78f604253), p7.

concepts.label: The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland
concepts.article_title: The auriculotemporal nerve's postganglionic route to the parotid gland
concepts.definition: Parasympathetic secretomotor supply to the parotid gland begins in the inferior salivatory nucleus and travels via the glossopharyngeal nerve, its tympanic branch, and the lesser petrosal nerve to synapse in the otic ganglion. From there, the auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, is the specific route by which these now-postganglionic parasympathetic fibres are distributed to the parotid gland; the auriculotemporal nerve is the classic "hitchhiking" pathway, carrying autonomic fibres it did not itself originate, alongside its own sensory fibres to the scalp and temporomandibular joint.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Parasympathetic pathways of the head
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the auriculotemporal nerve's role (carrying already-postganglionic fibres from the otic ganglion onward to the parotid gland) with the lesser petrosal nerve's role (carrying preganglionic fibres to the otic ganglion) — the two nerves are sequential legs of the same reflex arc, not interchangeable.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 20 ("auriculotemporal / Post ganglionic parasympathetic to Otic Ganglion"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 20 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2019.pdf (src_00b7644763f78f604253), p3.
